approachQuestion.prompt: Return the greatest number of characters that can appear in order in both strings a and b. Chosen characters need not be adjacent, and each original index can be used only once. Return only the length. Examples: a="axbyc", b="abc" → 3; a="aa", b="a" → 1; a="ab", b="ba" → 1. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ m=a.length,n=b.length ≤ 1500; lowercase letters; strings are read-only.

options.text: Keep two rows of n+1 lengths, initially zero. For prefix pair (i,j), when a[i−1]=b[j−1], use the preceding diagonal length plus one; otherwise use max(length above,length left). Reset column zero each row and swap row references.
options.feedback: Matching last characters can extend an optimal pair of shorter prefixes. If last characters differ, a common subsequence omits at least one of them, covered by above and left.

options.text: Compute the same prefix-pair recurrence but store the whole (m+1) by (n+1) table.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: When the last characters differ set the cell to zero; return the largest cell anywhere.
options.feedback: This enforces adjacency. For a="axbyc", b="abc", it returns 1 although the in-order nonadjacent answer is 3.

options.text: Count each letter’s minimum frequency in the two strings and sum those counts.
options.feedback: For a="ab", b="ba", this returns 2 while the order constraint permits only 1.

feedback.reason: Distinguish subsequences from contiguous matches using the mismatch transition.
details: Compute all m×n prefix pairs using two allocated n+1-entry rows and constant-time row-reference swaps, then return the final cell. Do not exchange the input strings or copy rows.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Compute all m×n prefix pairs using two allocated n+1-entry rows and constant-time row-reference swaps, then return the final cell. Do not exchange the input strings or copy rows. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=m+n; m,n vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Compute all prefix pairs with two rows of the stated column length.
details: Each prefix pair is computed once. Positive lengths make initialization dominated by mn. Two rows of length n+1 are retained; this fixed orientation does not choose the shorter string. There is no reconstruction, copying, hashing, or recursion.
“O(m+n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The recurrence computes every pair of nonempty prefix lengths, giving mn cells.
“O(mn) time, O(mn) auxiliary space”: Only the preceding row and current row are retained.
“O(mn) time, O(min(m,n)) auxiliary space”: The fixed method uses b for its columns and does not switch to the shorter input.
